l: death of Nephi, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Nephi becomes old, appoints a man king and ruler over his people, then dies; succeeding rulers retain his name as second Nephi, third Nephi, and so forth.

l: wives, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Tender, chaste wives are wounded and heartbroken by the Nephite people’s wickedness, abominations, and bad examples.

l: daughters of this people, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The daughters of this people, fair and tender, suffer sorrow from their husbands’ wickedness; God hears their mourning, protects them, and curses men who would lead them captive.

l: land of promise, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: abounds_in precious ores [most plentifully] The land of promise abounds plentifully in gold, silver, and all manner of precious ores.

l: scriptures, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Jacob declares that scriptures and prophets truly testify of Christ; after Sherem’s death, Nephi’s people search the scriptures and stop hearkening to Sherem.

l: commandments, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: prohibits whoredoms [except when the Lord commands otherwise to raise up seed] The people have known the commandments given to Lehi but have done things they ought not to have done. They must keep the commandments or the land will be cursed for their sakes.

l: pride, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_abominable God Pride causes some people to lift up their hearts, wear costly apparel, and persecute their brethren because they suppose they are better than others. Jacob condemns this pride and warns that it can destroy their souls.

l: riches, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Riches are obtained by Nephi’s people through providence and should follow seeking God’s kingdom, then serve the needy after hope in Christ.

l: whoredoms, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: are_an_abomination_before God Whoredoms are an abomination before God. The men are commanded to have no concubines and not to commit whoredoms like those of old.

l: chastity, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_delighting_to God [of women] God delights in the chastity of women.

l: the kingdom of God, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The kingdom of God must be sought before riches and saves those who will not harden their hearts.

l: the pure in heart, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The pure in heart are people urged to look to God and pray with firm, exceeding faith, receiving his word, feasting on his love, and continuing forever.

l: the filthy, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The filthy, people not pure in heart, are warned to repent or curse their inherited land; Lamanites will destroy them while God leads away the righteous.

l: the devil, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: deceives Sherem [as Sherem later confessed] The devil is identified as the source of Sherem’s flattering speech and as the power by which Sherem was deceived. Sherem confesses that he had been deceived by the power of the devil.

l: the land of inheritance, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The land of inheritance is cursed and possessed by the Lamanites unless the filthy repent; otherwise God leads away the righteous.

l: the commandment concerning marriage, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The commandment concerning marriage requires one wife, forbids concubines and whoredoms, and is observed by the Lamanites, so the Lord God will not destroy them.

l: God's love, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_a love [belonging to God] The pure in heart are invited to feast upon God's love. They may do so forever if their minds are firm.

l: justice, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Justice cannot be denied: those rejecting gospel warnings go into the lake of fire and brimstone.

l: the cursing of the Lamanites, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_a cursing [sore] The Lamanites are described as having a sore cursing, which is connected to the cursing that has come upon their skins. Despite this cursing, they are not filthy like the people of Nephi and observe the commandment concerning marriage.

l: destruction, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_a consequence [of sin and failure to repent] The Lamanites will scourge the filthy unto destruction if they do not repent. Filthiness may also bring the children of the people of Nephi unto destruction.

l: repentance, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Repentance is required of the filthy to prevent destruction, a cursed land, and loss to the Lamanites. Jacob urges my brethren to come with full purpose of heart and cleave unto God, leading through the narrow way to eternal life.

l: filthiness, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: causes destruction [of children through parental example] Filthiness causes the land to be cursed and can bring children unto destruction. Jacob commands the people of Nephi to remember their own filthiness and not revile the Lamanites because of theirs.

l: the darkness of their skins, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_a darkness [of the Lamanites' skins] The people of Nephi are commanded to revile no more against the Lamanites because of the darkness of their skins. They are told instead to remember their own filthiness.

l: the lake of fire and brimstone, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: A place of unquenchable flames, forever-ascending smoke, and endless torment, where those condemned by justice must go.

l: the plates, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The plates record the proceedings of the people of Nephi, including their wars, contentions, and kings’ reigns, while stating that even a hundredth part of those proceedings cannot be written upon them.

l: the plates of Jacob, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Plates made by Nephi’s hand, later identified by Jacob as the plates of Jacob at the end of his words.

l: Jews, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Jews are described as stiffnecked, rejecting plain words and prophets while seeking mystery; looking beyond the mark brings blindness and stumbling, though they may later build upon the sure foundation.

l: prophets, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Holy prophets before Christ’s coming believed in and testified of Christ, worshiped the Father in his name, hoped for his glory, and spoke through prophecy and revelation.

l: law of Moses, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The law of Moses is kept by Jacob’s people, sanctified to them for righteousness, and points souls to Christ. Sherem calls it God’s right way and accuses Jacob of changing it into worship of a future being; Jacob answers that the scriptures testify of Christ.

l: atonement of Christ, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The atonement of Christ is necessary for mankind: without it all must be lost. It reconciles people to God through Christ, enables resurrection, and presents them as Christ’s first-fruits unto God; Jacob testifies of it through the Holy Ghost.

l: resurrection, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Resurrection is associated with power in Christ, through which people may gain knowledge of it and the world to come; it brings those who reject warnings and the gospel before the bar of God with shame and awful guilt.

l: Spirit (God's spirit), The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The Spirit speaks truth, reveals reality, and provides revelations, prophecy, and understanding of things as they are and will be, leading Jacob to prophesy.

l: stone (sure foundation), The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The stone, the great and only sure foundation for the Jews to build on, is rejected before becoming head of their corner.

l: foundation, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_safe safe [for building] A safe foundation is associated with the stone that the Jews reject. The stone is described as the only sure foundation upon which they can build.

l: hope, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_of glory [in Christ] Jacob and the holy prophets have hope of Christ’s glory before his coming. Through witnesses, faith, and knowledge of Christ, people obtain a hope of glory before Christ manifests himself in the flesh.

l: coming of Christ, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_future_to prophets [many hundred years] Jacob’s people and the holy prophets knew of Christ and hoped for his glory many hundred years before his coming. Christ’s coming is described as his manifesting himself in the flesh.

l: the Lord, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The Lord is master of the vineyard, caring for its trees with diligent pruning, digging, nourishing, grafting, and watching. He values and seeks to preserve natural fruit for his purpose and glory, mourns corruption, and directs his servants to restore it. After sparing the vineyard, he sends servants in power to recover his people; good fruit is preserved, bad fruit cast away, and the vineyard ultimately burned.

l: servant of the Lord of the vineyard, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: A servant of the Lord of the vineyard obeys commands, grafts and nourishes trees, urges the Lord to spare the vineyard, explains failing roots, and later brings other servants to labor.

l: servants of the Lord of the vineyard, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The Lord’s few servants labor mightily in his vineyard, nourishing and pruning it, then go forth in his power at the last time.

l: the vineyard, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The vineyard, possessed by the Lord, contains olive trees and branches producing good and bad fruit. Once corrupt, it is repeatedly pruned, dug, nourished, dunged, and grafted by the Lord’s servants. After the final labor it bears natural fruit, is no longer corrupt, and becomes one body after the bad is cast away. It is ultimately burned in fire after the good and bad are separated.

l: tame olive-tree, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The tame olive-tree, in a nourished vineyard, grows old and decays. Its master prunes and nourishes it, removes main branches, grafts in wild branches, and plants natural branches elsewhere. With further care and grafting, its roots are preserved and natural fruit is restored.

l: wild olive-tree, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The wild olive-tree has wild branches. Its branches are grafted into the tame olive-tree, draw strength from its roots and initially bear tame fruit, then overrun the roots and produce evil fruit before removal or retention and grafting.

l: natural tree, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: A natural tree with branches and fruit is planted across a vineyard; branches become wild and corrupt, then are exchanged and grafted back, and continued labor restores strength and natural fruit.

l: my brethren, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Beloved brethren are urged to repent wholeheartedly, cleave unto God, and hear his voice; rejecting prophets, Christ, and his word brings shame and guilt before God.

l: mercy, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_extended my brethren [in the light of the day] God’s mercy is described as great, and his arm of mercy is extended toward my brethren in the light of the day.

l: the good word of God, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: nourishes my brethren [all the day long] The good word of God nourishes people all the day long. Those who bring forth evil fruit after being nourished must be hewn down and cast into the fire.

l: the Holy Ghost, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The Holy Ghost manifests Christ’s truth and the need for atonement to Jacob, then its power is confessed before the people.

l: the great plan of redemption, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The great plan of redemption is laid for brethren, who are warned not to make a mock of it.

l: redemption, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Redemption is in Christ; it brings gospel rejecters before God’s bar, where warnings rejected end in shame and awful guilt.

l: endless torment, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is endless The lake of fire and brimstone is identified as endless torment.

l: the strait gate, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_entered_by my brethren [through repentance] My brethren are urged to enter in at the strait gate.

l: the way which is narrow, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_continued_in my brethren [until they obtain eternal life] My brethren are urged to continue in the way which is narrow until they obtain eternal life.

l: eternal life, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_obtained_through the way which is narrow Eternal life is obtained by continuing in the way which is narrow after entering in at the strait gate.

l: the bar of God, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: The bar of God is where the speaker will meet my brethren, pleasing some but striking the wicked with dread and fear.

l: Sherem, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Sherem is a learned man among the people of Nephi who uses powerful, flattering speech to preach that there should be no Christ and seek to overthrow Christ’s doctrine. He contends with Jacob and asks for a sign, is struck by the Lord’s power, then confesses Christ, the Holy Ghost, and deception by the devil before fearing hell and dying.

l: Jacob, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: Jacob, a prophet among the Nephi people and father of Enos, has faith in Christ through angels, God’s voice, revelation, and the Holy Ghost. He testifies of Christ and the necessary atonement, confounds Sherem, prays for God’s will, and gives the plates to Enos.

l: faith in Christ, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_held_by Jacob [concerning Christ who should come] Jacob has faith in Christ who should come, based on revelations, visions of angels, and the voice of the Lord. Sherem seeks to shake Jacob from this faith but cannot do so.

l: Sherem's death, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: occurs_after Sherem's confession [when Sherem could say no more] After being struck by the power of the Lord, Sherem is nourished for many days and asks the people to gather so he can speak before he dies. He gives up the ghost after confessing the Christ and acknowledging his deception.

l: Sherem's confession, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: includes Christ [and the power of the Holy Ghost and ministering of angels] Sherem confesses before the people that he denied Christ, lied unto God, and had been deceived by the power of the devil. He also confesses Christ, the power of the Holy Ghost, and the ministering of angels.

l: peace and restoration, The Book of Jacob, the Brother of Nephi
s: is_restored_among people of Nephi [after Sherem's death] After Sherem’s death and confession, peace and the love of God are restored among the people. They search the scriptures and no longer listen to the words of Sherem.

l: The Book of Enos
s: Enos describes his struggle before God, receiving a remission of his sins through faith in Christ and then praying for the welfare of the Nephites and Lamanites. God promises to answer Enos according to his faith and covenants to preserve the records of the Nephites for the Lamanites in his own due time. Enos prophesies and testifies among the Nephites, whose efforts to restore the Lamanites to the true faith are unsuccessful. The chapter also describes the land, the peoples' conduct, wars between the Nephites and Lamanites, and Enos's expectation of rest with his Redeemer and of putting on immortality.

l: Enos, The Book of Enos
s: Enos learns from his father, hunts in the forests, prays all day and night, receives a remission of his sins, and then prays for the Nephites and Lamanites. He obtains God's promise concerning the records of the Nephites, prophesies and testifies among the people of Nephi, and looks forward to resting with his Redeemer and putting on immortality.

l: Enos's father, The Book of Enos
s: Enos's father was a just man who taught Enos in his language and in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. He and Enos's other fathers had required God to preserve the records, according to their faith.

l: God, The Book of Enos
s: God forgives Enos's sins, explains that his faith in Christ has made him whole, and promises to answer his desires. God gives the Nephites the land, preserves the records according to his covenant, and judges the peoples according to their diligence and iniquity.

l: Christ, The Book of Enos
s: Christ is the one in whom Enos has faith, although Enos has not yet heard or seen him. Christ will manifest himself in the flesh many years later.

l: Nephites, The Book of Enos
s: The Nephites seek to restore the Lamanites to the true faith, but their efforts are vain because the Lamanites' hatred is fixed. The Nephites till the land, raise crops and animals, have many prophets, and are kept from destruction by exceedingly plain preaching and prophesying.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Enos
s: The Lamanites are not destroyed, and Enos prays that they may someday receive the records of the Nephites and be brought unto salvation. Their hatred is fixed, they are described as wild and ferocious, and they continually seek to destroy the Nephites.

l: the land, The Book of Enos
s: God has given the land to the Nephites, and it is a holy land. God does not curse it except for the cause of iniquity.

l: records of the Nephites, The Book of Enos
s: Enos prays that the records of the Nephites will be preserved if his people are destroyed. God covenants to bring them forth to the Lamanites in his own due time.

l: the words of Enos's father, The Book of Enos
s: The words Enos had often heard his father speak concerning eternal life and the joy of the saints sink deep into Enos's heart and lead him to hunger spiritually.

l: eternal life, The Book of Enos
s: Enos's father taught him about eternal life, and those words help awaken Enos's desire for God.

l: sin, The Book of Enos
s: Enos struggles before God for a remission of his sins, and his guilt is swept away after God forgives him.

l: faith, The Book of Enos
s: Enos receives forgiveness because of his faith in Christ. His faith becomes unshaken, and God grants his desires and promises to preserve the records because of his faith.

l: prayer, The Book of Enos
s: Enos kneels before his Maker and cries unto God in mighty prayer and supplication all day and into the night. He later prays and labors for the Nephites, the Lamanites, and the preservation of the records.

l: remission of sins, The Book of Enos
s: Enos receives a remission of his sins after wrestling before God in prayer. God tells him that this occurs because of his faith in Christ.

l: forgiveness of sins, The Book of Enos
s: God tells Enos that his sins are forgiven, and Enos knows that God cannot lie, so his guilt is swept away.

l: God's covenant, The Book of Enos
s: God covenants with Enos that he will bring the records of the Nephites to the Lamanites in his own due time. Enos knows this will happen according to the covenant.

l: God's commandments, The Book of Enos
s: God will visit the Nephites according to their diligence in keeping his commandments. Their transgressions will be brought down with sorrow upon their own heads.

l: salvation, The Book of Enos
s: Enos desires that the records of the Nephites might be brought to the Lamanites so that perhaps they may be brought unto salvation.

l: wars between the Nephites and Lamanites, The Book of Enos
s: Enos sees wars between the Nephites and Lamanites during the course of his days.

l: preaching and prophesying, The Book of Enos
s: Enos preaches and prophesies according to the truth in Christ and declares the word throughout his days. Among the Nephites, exceedingly harsh preaching and prophesying about war, destruction, death, eternity, judgment, and God's power are needed to keep them from destruction.

l: immortality, The Book of Enos
s: Enos rejoices in the day when his mortal body will put on immortality and he will stand before God and see his face with pleasure.

l: The Book of Jarom
s: Jarom writes a brief record on small plates according to the commandment of his father, Enos, for the benefit of the Lamanites. The Nephites grow strong, keep the law of Moses and the commandments, defend themselves against the Lamanites, and become prosperous in the land. Prophets, priests, and teachers warn the people, teach the law of Moses, and persuade them to look forward to the Messiah, helping prevent their destruction. Jarom records years of wars, contentions, and dissensions before delivering the plates to his son Omni.

l: Jarom, The Book of Jarom
s: Jarom writes a brief record according to the commandment of his father, Enos. He does not write his prophesying or revelations, refers readers to the other plates of Nephi for records of wars, and delivers his plates to his son Omni.

l: Messiah, The Book of Jarom
s: The prophets, priests, and teachers persuade the people to look forward unto the Messiah and believe in him to come as though he already was.

l: Lord, The Book of Jarom
s: The Lord is the one whom the Nephites' kings and leaders serve in faith. The people observe the sabbath day holy unto the Lord, and the Lord's prophets threaten the people according to the word of God.

l: God, The Book of Jarom
s: God's word warns that the Nephites will be destroyed from the face of the land if they do not keep the commandments and fall into transgression.

l: Nephites, The Book of Jarom
s: The Nephites become strong, multiply, spread across the land, and grow rich in precious materials and workmanship. Their kings and leaders teach them the ways of the Lord, and they withstand and drive away the Lamanites.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Jarom
s: The Lamanites are more numerous than the Nephites, love murder, and drink the blood of beasts. They come many times against the Nephites in battle but do not prosper against them.

l: prophets, The Book of Jarom
s: The prophets warn the people of Nephi that transgression will lead to destruction. They labor diligently with priests and teachers to teach the law of Moses, testify of the Messiah, and stir the people to repentance.

l: land, The Book of Jarom
s: The Nephites are not swept from the face of the land because of God's mercy. They spread across the land, fortify their cities and places of inheritance, and are warned that disobedience would bring destruction from it.

l: plates, The Book of Jarom
s: Jarom writes on small plates so the genealogy may be kept and for the benefit of the Lamanites. He says the other plates of Nephi contain records of the wars and delivers his plates to Omni.

l: plan of salvation, The Book of Jarom
s: Jarom says that his fathers have revealed the plan of salvation, and he considers this sufficient to write about.

l: law of Moses, The Book of Jarom
s: The Nephites observe the law of Moses, and the prophets, priests, and teachers teach both the law and the intent for which it was given.

l: commandments, The Book of Jarom
s: The Nephites are taught that keeping the commandments brings prosperity in the land. They are warned that failing to keep them and falling into transgression will result in destruction.

l: wars, The Book of Jarom
s: Jarom says that much of the time through two hundred and thirty-eight years was occupied by wars, contentions, and dissensions. He directs readers to the other plates of Nephi for records of the wars.

l: battles, The Book of Jarom
s: The Lamanites come many times against the Nephites to battle. The Nephites withstand them and sweep them away from their lands.

l: destruction, The Book of Jarom
s: The prophets warn that the people will be destroyed from the face of the land if they do not keep the commandments. The people's teaching and repentance keep them from being destroyed during this period.

l: repentance, The Book of Jarom
s: The prophets, priests, and teachers continually stir the people up unto repentance by pricking their hearts with the word.

l: The Book of Omni
s: Omni, Amaron, Chemish, Abinadom, and Amaleki successively keep the plates and record warfare, judgments, transfers of the records, and teachings. Mosiah leads those who heed the Lord from the land of Nephi through the wilderness to the land of Zarahemla, where they discover and unite with the people of Zarahemla. The Lord preserves the righteous, gives Mosiah power to interpret engravings, and allows the Nephites to gain advantage over the Lamanites. Amaleki gives the plates to Benjamin and describes an unsuccessful attempt to return to the land of Nephi.

l: Omni, The Book of Omni
s: Omni was commanded by his father Jarom to write on the plates. He fought with the sword to preserve the Nephites from the Lamanites, acknowledged that he was wicked and had not kept the Lord’s commandments as he should, and delivered the plates to his son Amaron.

l: Amaron, The Book of Omni
s: Amaron wrote a few things in his father’s book. He recorded that after three hundred and twenty years the more wicked part of the Nephites had been destroyed, and he delivered the plates to his brother Chemish.

l: Chemish, The Book of Omni
s: Chemish wrote a few things in the same book as his brother Amaron. He confirmed that Amaron wrote his final record with his own hand when he delivered the plates to him.

l: Abinadom, The Book of Omni
s: Abinadom was the son of Chemish. He witnessed much war and contention between the Nephites and the Lamanites and killed many Lamanites with his sword in defense of his brethren.

l: Amaleki, The Book of Omni
s: Amaleki was the son of Abinadom and wrote about Mosiah, Benjamin, the people of Zarahemla, and an attempted return to the land of Nephi. Having no seed and knowing Benjamin was just before the Lord, Amaleki delivered the plates to him and exhorted people to come unto God and Christ.

l: Mosiah, The Book of Omni
s: Mosiah was warned by the Lord to flee the land of Nephi with those who would heed the Lord. He led them through the wilderness to the land of Zarahemla, became king after the people united, taught the people of Zarahemla his language, and interpreted engravings on a large stone by the gift and power of God.

l: Benjamin, The Book of Omni
s: Benjamin was the son of Mosiah and reigned in his stead. Amaleki described him as a just man before the Lord and delivered the plates to him.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Omni
s: Zarahemla was associated with the people discovered by Mosiah. He rejoiced greatly when the Lord sent Mosiah’s people with the plates of brass and gave a genealogy of his fathers from memory.

l: the Lord, The Book of Omni
s: The Lord warned Mosiah to flee the land of Nephi, led his people through the wilderness, and sent them to the people of Zarahemla with the plates of brass. The Lord brought judgment upon the wicked Nephites, spared the righteous, and gave Mosiah power to interpret engravings.

l: God, The Book of Omni
s: God is identified as the source of all that is good, while evil comes from the devil. Mosiah interpreted the engravings by the gift and power of God, and Amaleki exhorted people to come unto God, the Holy One of Israel.

l: the Nephites, The Book of Omni
s: The Nephites experienced seasons of peace, war, and bloodshed. The more wicked part of them was destroyed, while the righteous were spared, and under King Benjamin they gained much advantage over the Lamanites and drove them from the land of Zarahemla.

l: the Lamanites, The Book of Omni
s: The Lamanites were enemies of the Nephites. Abinadom killed many of them, and the Nephites later gained much advantage over them and drove them from the land of Zarahemla.

l: the people of Zarahemla, The Book of Omni
s: The people of Zarahemla were discovered by Mosiah’s people in the land of Zarahemla. They rejoiced at the arrival of Mosiah’s people, had come from Jerusalem in the time of Zedekiah, crossed the great waters, became numerous, suffered wars, lost their language and records, and united with Mosiah’s people.

l: the land of Nephi, The Book of Omni
s: The land of Nephi was the place from which Mosiah was warned by the Lord to flee. A considerable number later attempted to return to it but were slain in the wilderness except for fifty, who returned to the land of Zarahemla.

l: the wilderness, The Book of Omni
s: The wilderness was the route through which Mosiah’s people were led by the power of the Lord to the land of Zarahemla. It was also the place where the first attempted return to the land of Nephi ended in the deaths of all but fifty people.

l: the land of Zarahemla, The Book of Omni
s: The land of Zarahemla was where Mosiah’s people arrived and discovered the people of Zarahemla. The two peoples united there, Mosiah became their king, and King Benjamin drove the Lamanites out of it.

l: the plates, The Book of Omni
s: The plates preserved the genealogy and records of the people and were passed from Omni to Amaron, Chemish, Abinadom, and Amaleki. Amaleki delivered them to Benjamin when the plates were full.

l: the plates of brass, The Book of Omni
s: The plates of brass were carried by Mosiah’s people to the people of Zarahemla. They contained the record of the Jews and were a cause of great rejoicing among the people of Zarahemla.

l: the record of this people, The Book of Omni
s: The record of this people was engraved upon plates held by the kings according to the generations. Abinadom said that what was sufficient had been written and that he knew of no revelation or prophecy beyond what had been recorded.

l: genealogy, The Book of Omni
s: Genealogy was preserved on the plates. Zarahemla gave a genealogy of his fathers from memory, and the record of it was written but not on the plates.

l: the commandments of the Lord, The Book of Omni
s: The commandments of the Lord were not kept by Omni as he believed they should have been. The Lord’s judgment on the Nephites was tied to the warning that those who did not keep the commandments would not prosper in the land.

l: prophecy and revelation, The Book of Omni
s: Prophecy and revelation were included among the good things Amaleki urged people to believe in. Abinadom said he knew of no revelation or prophecy save what had been written.

l: salvation, The Book of Omni
s: Salvation was associated with coming unto Christ, the Holy One of Israel, and partaking of his salvation. Amaleki taught that those who continued in fasting and praying and endured to the end would be saved.

l: redemption, The Book of Omni
s: Redemption was described as a power found in Christ. Amaleki urged people to come unto Christ and partake of the power of his redemption.

l: war and bloodshed, The Book of Omni
s: War and bloodshed occurred repeatedly between the Nephites and the Lamanites. The unit records seasons of serious war, Abinadom’s killings, and a serious war during the reign of Benjamin.

l: the destruction of the Nephites, The Book of Omni
s: The more wicked part of the Nephites was destroyed after three hundred and twenty years had passed. The Lord nevertheless spared the righteous so that they would not perish.

l: the exodus of Mosiah's people, The Book of Omni
s: Mosiah’s people left the land of Nephi after Mosiah was warned by the Lord. Those who heeded the Lord were led through the wilderness by preaching, prophesying, continual admonition, and the power of the Lord’s arm to the land of Zarahemla.

l: the discovery of the people of Zarahemla, The Book of Omni
s: Mosiah’s people discovered the people of Zarahemla in the land of Zarahemla. Mosiah learned that they had come from Jerusalem in the time of Zedekiah, crossed the great waters, and had no records with them.

l: the union of the people of Zarahemla and Mosiah, The Book of Omni
s: The people of Zarahemla and Mosiah united together after Mosiah’s people taught them the language of Mosiah. Mosiah was appointed king over the united people.

l: the attempted return to the land of Nephi, The Book of Omni
s: A large number of people attempted to return to the land of Nephi to possess the land of their inheritance. Their strong and stiffnecked leader caused contention, all but fifty were slain in the wilderness, and the survivors returned to the land of Zarahemla; another group later departed, including Amaleki’s brother, whose fate was unknown.

l: The Words of Mormon
s: Mormon is about to deliver the record he has been making into the hands of his son Moroni after witnessing almost all the destruction of the Nephites. He finds plates containing an account from Jacob to the reign of king Benjamin and many of the words of Nephi, and he chooses to include them because of their prophecies concerning the coming of Christ. The records are preserved for a wise purpose, and Mormon prays that his brethren may return to the knowledge of God and the redemption of Christ. King Benjamin and the holy prophets establish peace after battles, contentions, false Christs, false prophets, and false teachers.

l: Mormon, The Words of Mormon
s: Mormon is about to deliver the record he has been making into the hands of his son Moroni. He has witnessed almost all the destruction of the Nephites, finds plates containing an account from Jacob to the reign of king Benjamin, and chooses to include them in his record.

l: Moroni, The Words of Mormon
s: Moroni is Mormon’s son and is to receive the record Mormon has been making. Mormon supposes that Moroni will witness the entire destruction of the Nephites, but prays that he may survive them and write concerning them and Christ.

l: Nephites, The Words of Mormon
s: The Nephites are Mormon’s people, and Mormon has witnessed almost all their destruction. Mormon prays that his brethren may once again become a delightsome people.

l: God, The Words of Mormon
s: God knows all things which are to come and works in Mormon according to his will. Mormon prays to God concerning his brethren and asks that the records be preserved.

l: Christ, The Words of Mormon
s: Christ is the subject of prophecies in the plates Mormon finds. Mormon hopes that Moroni may write concerning Christ, and he prays that his brethren may return to the redemption of Christ.

l: king Benjamin, The Words of Mormon
s: King Benjamin receives the plates from Amaleki, puts them with the other plates, and reigns over his people in righteousness. He gathers his armies against the Lamanites, fights with the sword of Laban, and, with the help of the holy prophets, establishes peace in the land.

l: Lamanites, The Words of Mormon
s: The Lamanites come down out of the land of Nephi to battle against king Benjamin’s people. King Benjamin and his armies contend against them, slay many thousands, and drive them out of all the lands of their inheritance.

l: record Mormon was making, The Words of Mormon
s: Mormon is about to deliver the record he has been making into the hands of Moroni. He finishes part of it from the plates of Nephi and says that he cannot write the hundredth part of the things of his people.

l: records, The Words of Mormon
s: Mormon searches among the records delivered into his hands and finds plates containing an account of prophets and many of the words of Nephi. The records are handed down from generation to generation, and Mormon prays that they will be preserved because great things are written upon them.

l: plates, The Words of Mormon
s: Mormon finds plates containing a small account of the prophets from Jacob down to the reign of king Benjamin and many of the words of Nephi. He chooses to take these plates and put them with the remainder of his record because they are choice to him and will be choice to his brethren.

l: plates of Nephi, The Words of Mormon
s: Mormon makes an abridgment from the plates of Nephi down to the reign of king Benjamin. He takes the remainder of his record from the plates of Nephi.

l: destruction of the Nephites, The Words of Mormon
s: Mormon has witnessed almost all the destruction of the Nephites. He supposes that Moroni will witness their entire destruction, and he prays that Moroni may survive them.

l: coming of Christ, The Words of Mormon
s: The plates please Mormon because they contain prophecies of the coming of Christ. Mormon says that many of these prophecies have been fulfilled and that the remaining things prophesied must come to pass.

l: reign of king Benjamin, The Words of Mormon
s: The account on the plates extends from Jacob down to the reign of king Benjamin. Mormon’s abridgment from the plates of Nephi also continues down to the reign of king Benjamin.

l: establishment of peace, The Words of Mormon
s: King Benjamin, with the assistance of the holy prophets among his people, establishes peace in the land. This follows battles against the Lamanites, false Christs, false prophets, false preachers and teachers, contentions, and dissensions.

l: prophecies, The Words of Mormon
s: The plates contain prophecies concerning the coming of Christ and concerning Mormon’s people down to that day and beyond it. Mormon says that many have been fulfilled and that those beyond that day must surely come to pass.

l: redemption of Christ, The Words of Mormon
s: Mormon prays that his brethren may once again come to the knowledge of the redemption of Christ. He hopes that they may once again become a delightsome people.

l: knowledge of God, The Words of Mormon
s: Mormon prays that his brethren may once again come to the knowledge of God. This prayer concerns their return to God and the redemption of Christ.

l: word of God, The Words of Mormon
s: The word of God is spoken with power and authority by holy men in the land. Records will be used to judge Mormon’s people and their brethren at the great and last day according to the word of God written upon them.

l: The Book of Mosiah
s: These records summarize the Book of Mosiah, beginning with King Benjamin preparing his son Mosiah to rule. Benjamin teaches his people that they owe everything to God, must serve one another, keep the commandments, repent, care for the needy, and receive salvation through Jesus Christ. An angel’s message foretells Christ’s ministry, suffering, death, resurrection, and atonement. The people experience a mighty change, covenant to obey God, take upon themselves the name of Christ, and Mosiah becomes king after Benjamin dies. Mosiah sends Ammon to learn the fate of Zeniff’s people in Lehi-Nephi. There Ammon finds King Limhi’s people oppressed by the Lamanites. Their history recounts Zeniff’s settlement, early prosperity, wars, and the later wicked reign of Noah. Noah rejects the prophet Abinadi, whose teachings condemn disobedience and proclaim that God will come among humanity, suffer, redeem his people, overcome death, and judge all according to their works. Alma accepts Abinadi’s words; Abinadi is burned to death, while Alma forms a church among believers. Noah’s people suffer invasion, bondage, and internal conflict. Limhi succeeds Noah, and, with Ammon and Gideon’s counsel, leads his people in a secret escape to Zarahemla. Alma’s community at Helam is likewise enslaved under Amulon and the former priests of Noah, but God strengthens and delivers them to Zarahemla. Mosiah reunites these groups; Alma baptizes Limhi’s people and organizes united churches. The final events address challenges within the church: unbelief among the rising generation, sin, discipline, and persecution. Alma receives authority to forgive repentant people and exclude those who refuse repentance. Alma the younger and the sons of Mosiah initially oppose the church but repent after an angel’s appearance and become missionaries. Mosiah’s sons leave to preach among the Lamanites, while Mosiah translates ancient records and entrusts them to Alma. Finally, because his sons refuse kingship and Mosiah warns of its dangers, the people replace kings with elected judges, making Alma the first chief judge and ending the reign of the kings.

l: king Benjamin, The Book of Mosiah
s: King Benjamin is a king, teacher, servant of God, and father of Mosiah, Helorum, and Helaman. During continual peace, he teaches his sons their fathers’ language, prophecies, records, commandments, and the Lord’s dealings. Old and subject to infirmities, he prepares Mosiah to rule by giving him charge over the kingdom and its records, including the sword of Laban and the ball or director. He gathers his people and, serving them with all his might, mind, and strength, teaches service, obedience, repentance, accountability, God’s goodness and power, salvation through the atonement, faith, care for the poor, and steadfast good works. He says he can no longer be their teacher or king and seeks to be blameless before God concerning them. After learning that the people believe his words, he accepts their covenant, teaches them to become children of Christ and take upon themselves the name of Christ, and records those who covenant with God. He consecrates Mosiah as ruler and king, appoints priests to teach the people, dismisses the multitude, lives three more years, and dies. His last words are also taught to the people of king Limhi through Ammon.

l: Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah
s: Mosiah, son of king Benjamin, becomes king and ruler over the people and receives from his father the records, plates of Nephi, sword of Laban, and ball or director. He proclaims his kingship and calls the people to gather. As king of Zarahemla, he receives Alma and Alma’s people with joy, grants his people liberty, and gives Alma authority over the church, including judgment of accused members. As unbelief and dissensions increase, he asks whether the people want a king and warns them in writing about unrighteous kings. He establishes judges, brings peace throughout the land, reigns until his death at sixty-three, and is succeeded as ruler.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah
s: The Lord is God, the Lord our God, an omnipotent and eternal ruler, creator, Redeemer, judge, and giver of laws and commandments. He preserves, supports, teaches, prospers, blesses, and delivers his people when they keep his commandments, trust him, call on him in faith and sincerity, confess, and repent. He gives the kingdom, records, the ball or director, teachers, rulers, life, peace, the Spirit of God, forgiveness, mercy, and eternal life to believers who endure. He establishes the church of God and promises that transgression alone can overthrow it. From the beginning, the Lord delivers prophecies and commandments to the fathers, preserves them by marvelous power, and brings the people out of Jerusalem and from enemies. He promises prosperity for obedience but warns that wickedness brings abandonment, hindered prosperity, destruction, bondage, and affliction. Through Abinadi, he calls Noah’s people to repent and declares punishments including famine, pestilence, hail, the east wind, insects, and destruction if they remain hardened. Yet he promises to hear and deliver those who repent and cry mightily. The Lord Omnipotent is said to come down from heaven among the children of men in a tabernacle of clay, work miracles, take upon himself the sins of the world, judge the world, and provide salvation. He grants forgiveness, pours out his Spirit, and redeems those who recognize him. He strengthens and delivers Alma’s people, softens the Lamanites, hears Alma after tribulation, and delivers people from bondage. He later works upon and spares the sons of Mosiah, permits their preaching among the Lamanites, promises belief and eternal life to many, and preserves interpreters so iniquities and abominations may be discovered. The whole record presents the Lord’s justice toward transgression and mercy, deliverance, and eternal life toward repentance and trust.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah
s: Zarahemla is a land, the origin of Ammon and his brethren, where Benjamin’s people end contention and live peacefully under a just king. Mosiah summons its people to the temple. Limhi’s searchers fail to find it, but Limhi’s people later arrive and join Mosiah’s people; Alma’s people also arrive. It contains the people of Nephi and Zarahemla, where Alma establishes churches.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_redeemed the Lord [the Lord has comforted his people] Jerusalem is told to break forth into joy because the Lord has comforted and redeemed his people. Waste places of Jerusalem are called to sing together.

l: wilderness, The Book of Mosiah
s: Wilderness contains king Noah’s priests, who flee Nephi, take Lamanite daughters, and remain there; forty-three lost travelers diligently seek Zarahemla but return to Limhi’s land.

l: the people, The Book of Mosiah
s: A people belonging to king Benjamin, dwelling in Zarahemla and later gathered at the temple throughout the land. Though exceedingly multiplied and too numerous to number, they assemble with their families, offer sacrifices and burnt offerings according to the law of Moses, and hear king Benjamin’s teachings about serving one another and keeping God’s commandments. They collectively believe his words, receive truth through the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, undergo a mighty change of heart, and experience great joy. Willingly they covenant with God to do his will and keep his commandments, take upon themselves the name of Christ, and become children of Christ. They are taught to retain that name in their hearts, remain steadfast and immovable in good works, and thereby receive salvation, eternal life, and heaven through Christ rather than torment or God’s wrath. Except for little children, they enter this covenant, return to their houses by families, and have no contention for three years. They have continual peace for the remainder of king Benjamin’s days.

l: the people of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people of Zarahemla are descendants of Mulek who came into the wilderness and dwell in the land. More numerous than the descendants of Nephi, they are numbered with the Nephites and gather with them at the temple to hear king Benjamin’s words.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah
s: The Lamanites are a people and brethren of the people of Nephi, portrayed as numerous, strong, and often hostile toward the Nephites. They know little of the Lord, records, and mysteries of God according to their fathers’ traditions, are described as lazy, idolatrous, sinful, and polluted, and depend on their own strength in battle. They hold an eternal hatred toward the children of Nephi, seek bondage for Nephite labor, and repeatedly fight, plunder, kill, capture, and impose heavy tribute and burdens. They attack Zeniff’s people, Noah’s people, and Limhi’s people; although often defeated or driven away, they surround Limhi’s people, keep them in bondage, and pursue their escape. At times their hearts soften: they show compassion to captives, become pacified toward Limhi’s people, and ease their burdens. They take possession of Helam and later Shemlon, Shilom, and Amulon, guarding Alma’s people after breaking a promise of liberty. They increase in riches and trade, learn the language of Nephi, and become cunning and wise in worldly wisdom while delighting in wickedness and plunder except among their own brethren. More than twice as numerous as the people of Nephi, they become the people to whom the sons of Mosiah preach, hoping to give them knowledge of the Lord, end their hatred, and establish friendship.

l: the plates of brass, The Book of Mosiah
s: The plates of brass contain records and commandments of God, preserved by the Lord and enabling understanding of the mysteries of God. King Benjamin says they prevent ignorance and unbelief; King Mosiah keeps and preserves them, then confers them on Alma the younger.

l: the plates of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah
s: The plates of Nephi contain true records and sayings of the fathers from their departure from Jerusalem onward. King Benjamin affirms their truth before the people, and King Mosiah preserves them among his records before conferring them upon Alma the younger.

l: the records, The Book of Mosiah
s: The records, preserved by God and engraved on brass plates, contain teachings, commandments, and fathers’ sayings; King Benjamin directs his sons to search and Mosiah to guard them.

l: the commandments of God, The Book of Mosiah
s: The commandments of God are commandments contained in the plates of brass, delivered through records, taught by Mosiah and Abinadi, and to be observed throughout life. They require obedience in all things, including rejecting graven images and avoiding sin such as killing, adultery, stealing, false witness, and coveting. Their central promise is blessedness, prosperity, protection, salvation, and a part in the first resurrection for those who keep them; transgression brings rebellion, separation from the Spirit of the Lord, perishing, and exclusion from that resurrection. King Benjamin’s people covenant to obey them for the rest of their days, and the church of God is exhorted to keep them with long-suffering and much travail. Abinadi refuses to deny them even unto death, while the rebellious knowingly refuse them. The account ends with Alma and his companions exhorting the church to keep them, and Mosiah teaching that kings should establish and obey them, though unrighteous kings may trample them.

l: the mysteries of God, The Book of Mosiah
s: are_understood_through the plates of brass The mysteries of God can be read and understood through the preserved records. King Benjamin teaches his sons that the plates help the people know these mysteries.

l: the kingdom, The Book of Mosiah
s: The kingdom is conferred by king Benjamin upon Mosiah, who receives charge of all its affairs; it is restricted to descendants of Nephi.

l: the name given to the people, The Book of Mosiah
s: A name King Benjamin intends to give his people, distinguishing them above those brought from Jerusalem; it endures and is not blotted out except through transgression.

l: the temple, The Book of Mosiah
s: The temple is a gathering and assembly place where people are commanded to hear king Benjamin. They gather and pitch tents facing it; when the multitude cannot fit within its walls, a tower is erected so they can hear him.

l: peace, The Book of Mosiah
s: Peace is a condition in the land, restored after persecution and established by Mosiah throughout the land. Prophets and others publish it as good tidings of good and salvation; continual peace exists after Alma becomes chief judge.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah
s: Sin is transgression, rebellion, ignorance, wickedness, abominations, and failures to repent, aid those in need, keep agreements, watch one’s thoughts, words, and deeds, and obey God’s commandments. It can make the Lord’s favored people wicked and adulterous, remove preservation and strength, blot out Christ’s name from transgressors’ hearts, withdraw the Spirit of the Lord, and prevent the Lord from succoring his people. Persistent, unrepentant sin leaves a person an enemy to God, brings guilt and anguish, and results in perishing; those who wilfully rebel and die in their sins are not redeemed or part of the first resurrection. Sin also brings communal consequences: it led people to bondage and affliction, and Noah’s flattering words caused his people to become sinful and idolatrous. An unrighteous king can cause many people’s sins through his iniquities. Yet repentance and faith in the Lord Jesus Christ are necessary for salvation, and the servant’s soul is offered for sin while the Son bears the sins and transgressions of those he redeems.

l: the proclamation of Mosiah's kingship, The Book of Mosiah
s: Mosiah proclaims throughout the land that he is king and ruler over the people whom the Lord has given them.

l: the gathering at the temple, The Book of Mosiah
s: The gathering at the temple is commanded and proclaimed so the people of Zarahemla, the people of Mosiah, and their families may hear king Benjamin. They assemble to receive his teachings as he gives final instructions and seeks to be found blameless before God.

l: Mosiah's succession, The Book of Mosiah
s: Mosiah's succession is Benjamin's planned transfer of the kingdom to his son Mosiah, who is declared king and ruler. Benjamin announces Mosiah's authority and links the people's prosperity to obeying Mosiah's and God's commandments.

l: Mosiah (Benjamin's son), The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a king [and ruler over the people] Mosiah carries out what his father commanded and makes a proclamation throughout the land. King Benjamin declares that Mosiah is a king and ruler over the people and instructs them to keep his commandments and the commandments of God delivered through him.

l: little children, The Book of Mosiah
s: Little children are blessed and blameless before God; Christ’s blood atones for their sins, and those who die in infancy do not perish.

l: the prophets, The Book of Mosiah
s: The prophets are holy messengers sent by God among all people. Since the world began, they have proclaimed Christ’s coming through signs, wonders, types, and shadows, publishing peace and good tidings. Those who prophesy of the Lord without transgression are the seed of the Lord and, with obedient believers, shall come forth in the first resurrection.

l: land, The Book of Mosiah
s: A land of liberty and equality, where people multiply and prosper through keeping commandments, receive protection from enemies, and may enjoy equal rights and privileges while permitted to inherit it.

l: tower near the temple, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_erected the temple [because the multitude was too great for the temple walls] A tower is erected because king Benjamin cannot teach the entire multitude within the temple walls. He speaks from the tower, and his words are written and sent to those who cannot hear him.

l: the law of Moses, The Book of Mosiah
s: The law of Moses is a strict law given by the Lord through Moses at Sinai to the children of Israel, appointed because they were stiffnecked, quick to do iniquity, and slow to remember the Lord. It requires daily performances, ordinances, and commandments, including worshiping no other God and making no graven images. Its signs, wonders, types, and shadows point to things to come. Though priests claim salvation comes by it, it provides no salvation and avails nothing without the Atonement of Jesus Christ; eventually it would no longer be expedient to keep.

l: the evil spirit, The Book of Mosiah
s: The evil spirit tempts people into sin; those obeying and remaining in sins become enemies to righteousness and receive punishment.

l: Spirit of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah
s: A spirit that guides people in wisdom’s paths, enticing the natural man to yield and become a saint. It may be withdrawn through transgression and rebellion. It comes upon Alma in prayer, fills Alma, Helam, and a multitude with joy and grace, and is poured out through baptism and upon people who joined the churches of God, blessing and prospering them.

l: divine justice, The Book of Mosiah
s: awakens damnation and punishment [in the unrepentant sinner] Divine justice awakens the immortal soul of an unrepentant enemy of God to a lively sense of guilt. This produces shrinking from the Lord's presence and fills the person with guilt, pain, and anguish.

l: heaven, The Book of Mosiah
s: Heaven is a place above the earth where faithful commandment-keepers dwell with God in never-ending happiness.

l: king Benjamin's speech, The Book of Mosiah
s: King Benjamin's speech is written for people beyond his voice, teaching service as service to God, indebtedness, obedience and blessings, and warning of rebellion, sin, evil, and unrepentant transgression.

l: service to one another, The Book of Mosiah
s: is service of God [when serving fellow beings] Service to others is taught to be service to God. King Benjamin says that because he has labored to serve the people, they should likewise labor to serve one another.

l: everlasting punishment, The Book of Mosiah
s: Everlasting punishment is the final doom of the unrepentant enemy of God: never-ending torment and endless damnation. It comes to those who obey the evil spirit, remain in sin, refuse humility and repentance, or follow carnal wills. They drink damnation to their souls, face their guilt and misery, are consigned to torment and a lake of fire and brimstone, and are delivered to the devil.

l: blessedness and prosperity, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_received_in heaven [by those faithful to the end] Those who keep the commandments of God are blessed in all things, both temporal and spiritual. If they remain faithful to the end, they are received into heaven to dwell with God in never-ending happiness, and they prosper in the land.

l: the angel, The Book of Mosiah
s: An angel from God declares joyful tidings to the speaker, teaching Christ’s coming, salvation through Jesus Christ, judgment, and the wicked’s fate.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah
s: God is a deity, Lord, Almighty God, and the one God, the Eternal Father of heaven and earth, above all things. He created heaven, earth, and all things, with all wisdom and power, and people depend on him for life and possessions. He hears prayers, answers faithful requests, knows hearts, grants remission of sins, gives commandments and the law of Moses, provides power for miracles, and makes covenants with people who promise to obey him. He is just, jealous, merciful to those who love and keep his commandments, and visits iniquity upon those who hate him. God is identified with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and preserves, feeds, leads, protects, and delivers his people: Israel from Egypt, fathers from Jerusalem, Zeniff’s people from enemies, and Alma’s people from bondage and affliction. He eases burdens, provides escape, and is thanked for immediate goodness and power. Through prophets, angels, commandments, and judgment, God addresses sin and salvation. God himself comes down among the children of men in the flesh, makes atonement, redeems his people and all mankind from a fallen state, breaks death’s bands, brings resurrection, and judges the dead according to their works. People are called to trust, serve, worship, humble themselves, cry to him, be born of God, become righteous, and seek eternal life through Christ.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah
s: Christ is identified as the Son of God, the Father of heaven and earth, the Creator of all things from the beginning, God and Father of all things, the very Eternal Father, the light of the world, and endless life. He creates heaven and earth, has the image after which man was created, and comes among the children of men by taking on flesh and blood, born of Mary. Though he comes unto his own, people consider him a man, accuse him of having a devil, reject, mock, scourge, crucify, and slay him. In the flesh he is subject to the Father and suffers temptation without yielding. The Lord lays the iniquities of all upon the servant; Christ takes sin upon himself as an offering, satisfies justice, and makes redemption possible. After death he rises, gains victory over death, overcomes the grave and its sting, makes intercession for the children of men, ascends into heaven, and judges the world. Through faith on his name, his atonement brings salvation and forgiveness: he spiritually begets covenant people, makes them free, seals them as his through good works, and may bring them to heaven. People take upon themselves his name and join the churches of God, although the rising generation does not believe concerning his coming.

l: Adam, The Book of Mosiah
s: Adam’s transgression causes people to fall and die. His fall is used as an example of justice and the consequences of partaking of forbidden fruit.

l: the people, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people are taught of Christ, salvation, repentance, faith, and judgment, yet remain stiffnecked, harden their hearts, and fail to understand the law of Moses through Christ’s atonement.

l: the natural man, The Book of Mosiah
s: The natural man is an enemy to God from Adam’s fall, remaining so unless he yields to the Holy Spirit, puts off the natural man, and becomes a saint through Jesus Christ’s Atonement.

l: coming of Christ, The Book of Mosiah
s: The coming of Christ is declared by an angel, prophets, signs, wonders, types, and shadows. Christ will come among the children of men in flesh and blood, though one prophet is killed for teaching it; knowledge of the Savior eventually spreads to every people.

l: the ministry of Jesus Christ, The Book of Mosiah
s: The ministry of Jesus Christ unfolds through mighty miracles: healing the sick, raising the dead, enabling the lame, blind, and deaf, curing diseases, and casting out devils.

l: the crucifixion and death of Christ, The Book of Mosiah
s: Jesus Christ suffers temptation, pain, hunger, thirst, fatigue, and anguish that brings blood from every pore. Considered a man and accused of having a devil, he is scourged, led, crucified, and slain. His flesh becomes subject to death; his will yields to the Father’s, taking iniquity and transgressions to redeem his people.

l: the resurrection of the dead, The Book of Mosiah
s: The resurrection of the dead is a real, prophesied event made possible when Christ rises on the third day and breaks the bands of death. The Messiah, the Son of God, brings it to pass through power over the dead. A first resurrection includes those who shall dwell with God through Christ; ultimately the dead stand before the bar of God to be judged according to their works.

l: the Atonement of Jesus Christ, The Book of Mosiah
s: The Atonement of Jesus Christ, prepared from the foundation of the world, is made by God himself through his blood. It atones for Adam’s transgression and for sins, including ignorant sin and those who died without knowing God’s will; it blesses infants and little children, brings salvation to those who endure in faith, and prevents God’s people from perishing.

l: the Fall of Adam, The Book of Mosiah
s: The Fall of Adam is Adam’s partaking of the forbidden fruit after the old serpent beguiled the first parents. It causes people to fall by nature, makes the natural man an enemy to God, and leaves all mankind carnal, sensual, and devilish.

l: salvation, The Book of Mosiah
s: Salvation comes only through Jesus Christ, through repentance, faith, and the atonement prepared for all mankind. It is everlasting and is received through Christ’s wisdom, power, justice, and mercy. It requires faith continued to the end of life, repentance, and keeping the commandments of God; it does not come through the law alone, because without the atonement people would perish notwithstanding the law of Moses. Salvation is not received by those who knowingly rebel against God, die in their sins, or refuse to keep his commandments. Through the Lord’s redemption it is granted and declared to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people. In the future, every nation, kindred, tongue, and people will see it and confess that God’s judgments are just, while it is believed in by seed and by those who will suffer death by fire.

l: repentance and faith, The Book of Mosiah
s: are_required_for salvation [on the Lord Jesus Christ] Repentance and faith on the Lord Jesus Christ are required for salvation. People must humble themselves, become as little children, and believe in salvation through Christ’s atoning blood.

l: Final Judgment, The Book of Mosiah
s: Final Judgment is the last-day judgment of all people, executed by Jesus Christ or the Redeemer. Every person, mortal and corrupt, stands before God and is judged justly according to works, good or evil. Words taught become a bright testimony at judgment. Those who live without God confess the justice of everlasting punishment and tremble beneath his all-searching eye.

l: mercy, The Book of Mosiah
s: Mercy extends its arms to all mankind, including those warned of iniquity, but the wicked who refuse to depart or call upon the Lord lose any claim forever.

l: justice, The Book of Mosiah
s: Justice denies mercy to wicked forever, claims rebellious knowing sinners; Son stands between men and justice, takes iniquity, satisfies its demands.

l: hell, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a lake of fire and brimstone [with unquenchable flames] The wicked are described as entering a state of misery and endless torment from which they can no more return. Their torment is compared to a lake of fire and brimstone with unquenchable flames and smoke ascending forever and ever.

l: Son of God, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a God The people believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who created heaven and earth and all things and shall come among the children of men.

l: children of men, The Book of Mosiah
s: are mankind The children of men are the people among whom God shall come down. The Son suffers and makes intercession for them, takes upon himself their iniquity and transgressions, and shows compassion toward them.

l: all mankind, The Book of Mosiah
s: All mankind, fallen, became carnal, sensual, devilish, and subject to the devil, knowing evil from good. Without God's redemption it would be endlessly lost; through atonement, trusting the Lord, and keeping commandments, it receives salvation, resurrects immortal and incorruptible, then stands before God for judgment.

l: the devil, The Book of Mosiah
s: The devil, God’s enemy, has power over the wicked who remain carnal and rebellious, subjecting them through their desires and receiving those delivered to him in endless damnation.

l: man, The Book of Mosiah
s: Man is a mortal, fallen, dependent body who relies on God and must believe, repent, keep commandments, humble himself, guard his conduct, and care for the poor throughout life.

l: poor, The Book of Mosiah
s: The poor are people without enough to remain day to day; those with sufficient should give, while those without remain guiltless if willing, and coveting what they lack is condemned.

l: beggar, The Book of Mosiah
s: needs substance [so that he may not perish] The beggar may ask for substance so that he does not perish. Those who deny him when they have the means to help are condemned.

l: kingdom of God, The Book of Mosiah
s: The kingdom of God is an inheritance for the seed of the Lord who believe the prophets and seek remission of sins; those refusing mercy to the miserable must repent or perish forever without interest in it.

l: remission of sins, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people receive a remission of their sins after calling on God in faith, and they experience joy and peace of conscience. They are taught to retain a remission of their sins by remembering God, remaining humble, praying daily, and serving others.

l: faith, The Book of Mosiah
s: Faith is in Jesus Christ and in what king Benjamin taught. It brings forgiveness, joy, peace of conscience, great knowledge, and changed hearts, making people sons and daughters of Christ. Alma preached faith on the Lord, the church was commanded to have one faith, and people must continue in it through testing and until the end of life.

l: repentance, The Book of Mosiah
s: Repentance is required for remission of sins, salvation through Christ, baptism, and forgiveness. It involves forsaking sins, humility before God, sincere prayer and confession, and, in one call, sackcloth, ashes, and crying mightily to the Lord. Abinadi calls Noah’s people to repent; Alma repents himself, teaches it, and commands priests to preach it. Throughout the churches, repentance and faith in God are preached. Those who sincerely repent after transgression may be forgiven and received through baptism, while those who refuse to repent perish forever or are excluded from the Lord’s people.

l: goodness of God, The Book of Mosiah
s: awakens man [to a sense of nothingness and fallen worthlessness] Knowledge of the goodness of God awakens people to their nothingness and fallen state. His goodness, power, wisdom, patience, and long-suffering are to be remembered continually.

l: substance, The Book of Mosiah
s: Substance belongs to God, includes food, raiment, gold, and silver, and is received by people to share wisely with the poor through feeding, clothing, visiting the sick, and providing relief.

l: coming of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a future_event [to be believed in until the end of life] The people are to continue in faith concerning the coming of the Lord, which was spoken by the mouth of the angel. They must remain faithful to the end of their lives.

l: care for the needy, The Book of Mosiah
s: Care for the needy is a commanded duty to give substance and answer beggars’ needs, unfolding through feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and providing spiritual and temporal relief.

l: Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, The Book of Mosiah
s: The Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent works a mighty change in king Benjamin’s people, changing their hearts and removing their disposition to do evil.

l: children of Christ, The Book of Mosiah
s: is_a sons and daughters of Christ Those who make the covenant with God are called the children of Christ, his sons and daughters, because Christ spiritually begets them and their hearts are changed through faith on his name.

l: covenant, The Book of Mosiah
s: The covenant with God is a righteous commitment to do his will, serve him with all one’s heart, and keep his commandments for the remainder of life. King Benjamin connects it with becoming children of Christ, and the people enter it by taking upon themselves Christ’s name. Alma’s people seek God’s fold and, through baptism, covenant to serve him and keep his commandments until death. Ammon, his brethren, Limhi, and many of Limhi’s people also enter it. God recognizes Alma’s people’s covenant, promises to covenant with his people, and deliver them from bondage.

l: mighty change of heart, The Book of Mosiah
s: The mighty change of heart is wrought by the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent. It removes the disposition to do evil and gives king Benjamin’s people a disposition to do good continually.

l: the name of Christ, The Book of Mosiah
s: The name of Christ is the only name that brings salvation. Those who covenant with God take it upon themselves, retain it in their hearts, join the churches of God, and become the people of God. Transgression can blot it out; knowing it determines right or left hand of God.

l: eternal life, The Book of Mosiah
s: Eternal life is promised and given through Christ to the redeemed, little children, prophets in the first resurrection, and those with good works; it brings everlasting salvation, heaven, endless life, and happiness.

l: evil, The Book of Mosiah
s: leads_to endless damnation [at the resurrection] King Benjamin’s people say that the change wrought in them has removed their disposition to do evil and made them desire to do good continually. They are also instructed to remain steadfast and abound in good works.

l: king Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah
s: Mosiah is a ruler and king over the people, consecrated by king Benjamin and beginning his reign in his father’s stead at thirty. He observes the Lord’s judgments and statutes, keeps the commandments, appoints priests to teach, and tills the earth so he will not burden his people. After three years of peace, he authorizes sixteen strong men led by Ammon to inquire about people who had gone to dwell in the land of Lehi-Nephi. Mosiah is also a seer, revelator, and prophet with a gift from God to interpret engravings and translate records by means of interpreters. He gathers the people and has Zeniff’s records and Alma’s account read to them, then grants Alma authority to establish churches and ordain priests and teachers throughout Zarahemla. He prohibits persecution of church members and commands equality, humility, and labor for support. When his sons seek to preach among the Lamanites, he inquires of the Lord and grants their request. With none of his sons accepting the kingdom, he gives the records and interpreters to Alma the younger, commanding him to preserve them and keep a record of the people.

l: kingdom, The Book of Mosiah
s: belongs_to Aaron [rightfully, but he declines it] The kingdom rightly belongs to Mosiah’s son, but he declines it, and none of Mosiah’s sons is willing to take it upon himself.

l: the people of Zeniff, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people of Zeniff leave Zarahemla to dwell in Lehi-Nephi, then send no word back, causing Mosiah’s people continual concern.

l: land of Lehi-Nephi, The Book of Mosiah
s: The land of Lehi-Nephi is land once possessed by the Nephites. Ammon and sixteen men seek it from Zarahemla, wandering forty days before arriving. King Laman grants it to Zeniff, whose people possess it. After failed battles, Limhi and his people return and dwell there, and Limhi is taken there after Ammon and his brethren are discovered.

l: city of Lehi-Nephi, The Book of Mosiah
s: City in the land of Lehi-Nephi, yielded by king Laman to Zeniff, later held by Limhi’s people in Lamanite bondage.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah
s: The land of Zarahemla sends Ammon and fifteen men to seek people who had left, while others unsuccessfully search for it. Alma and his people later arrive there and are joyfully received by King Mosiah. The reign of the judges then begins throughout it among the Nephites.

l: Ammon, The Book of Mosiah
s: Ammon is a strong and mighty man from the land of Zarahemla who leads sixteen men to seek their brethren in the land of Nephi. With Amaleki, Helem, and Hem, he is captured, imprisoned for two days, then released and welcomed by king Limhi after identifying himself. He recounts Zarahemla’s history and explains king Benjamin’s teachings to Limhi’s people. He explains that their king can translate ancient records through a God-given gift, though he himself cannot translate languages. Ammon rejoices that the engravings can be interpreted, mourns Abinadi and the losses among their people, and refuses to baptize because he considers himself unworthy. Finally, he consults on escape from bondage and leads Limhi’s people and his brethren toward Zarahemla.

l: land of Shilom, The Book of Mosiah
s: Land possessed by the Nephites: King Laman grants it to Zeniff, whose people repair Shilom’s walls and cultivate it. Noah later builds there and overlooks it from towers. During Limhi’s escape, his people travel around it in the wilderness.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah
s: The land of Nephi is a land containing the city of Nephi and associated with the fathers’ first inheritance. Zeniff’s people journey there, settle it, inherit it for twenty-two years, prosper, and have continual peace, though the Lamanites attack them; Zeniff’s people drive the attackers out and return to the land. Later, Limhi’s people dwell there under Lamanite oppression, and captured people are carried back there before returning after learning their wives and children were not slain. Searchers return there after failing to find Zarahemla and after finding a destroyed, peopled land. Ammon and three brethren go down there, meet the king’s guard, and are imprisoned. The Lamanites and Amulon seek it, and the sons of Mosiah seek permission to go there to preach to the Lamanites.

l: Limhi, The Book of Mosiah
s: Limhi is a just king, son of Noah, made king by the voice of the people and ruling the people in the land of Nephi and Shilom. After captivity and his father’s iniquities, the people confer the kingdom on him; he establishes peace, defends his people when the Lamanites prepare for war, refuses to kill their captured king, and seeks the truth about the abduction. He returns to the city of Nephi, permits battle, supports widows and children, and sends men to search for Zarahemla. When Ammon arrives, Limhi learns that their brethren in Zarahemla are alive, tells his people, receives their history, and presents plates containing his people’s record for translation. He encourages trust in God, covenants to serve God and keep his commandments, and desires baptism. Under an oath with the king of the Lamanites, he consults Ammon and his people about deliverance, accepts Gideon’s plan, sends wine as a present, and leads his people away by night. Alma later baptizes him into the church of God.

l: king Noah, The Book of Mosiah
s: King Noah, son of Zeniff, reigns in Zeniff’s stead but rejects his father’s ways. He does not keep the commandments of God, follows his own desires, takes many wives and concubines, and leads his people into sin. He taxes them heavily to support himself, his household, and proud new priests, while removing the priests consecrated by his father. He builds elegant buildings, a spacious palace, temple work, and high towers; plants vineyards, makes abundant wine, lives riotously, and values riches. He sends guards against the Lamanites and armies against them. When Abinadi speaks against his rule, Noah grows angry, commands that Abinadi be seized and slain, imprisons him, and directs his priests to question, remove, and kill him. Though he briefly fears Abinadi’s words and God’s judgments, his priests stir him back to anger, and Abinadi is delivered to death. Noah also accuses Alma of rebellion and sends an army after Alma and the people of the Lord. His rule oppresses Alma’s people through bondage under Noah and his priests. During a Lamanite attack, Noah flees, leads his people into the wilderness, orders the men to abandon their wives and children, and is eventually captured by his people and killed by fire.

l: Zeniff, The Book of Mosiah
s: Zeniff, a Nephite, comes from Zarahemla seeking to inherit his fathers’ land and is made king over his people in the land of Nephi. Sent as a spy among the Lamanites, he sees good in them and opposes their destruction. His over-zealous desire for the land leads king Laman to deceive him and secure Lehi-Nephi and Shilom. Zeniff nevertheless obtains permission to occupy those lands, establishes and defends his kingdom, prepares his people for battle, and leads them against the Lamanites. In old age he teaches trust in the Lord and gives the kingdom to his son Noah.

l: the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah
s: The people of Limhi are Nephites living in the land of Nephi under king Limhi. They are fewer than the Lamanites, held in bondage, and compelled to pay grievous tribute. Limhi gathers them at the temple, teaches that their iniquities brought their afflictions, and urges them to turn to God. After hearing Ammon recount the history of their brethren and the words of king Benjamin, they endure an attack arising from the Lamanites’ belief that they abducted their daughters; they defend themselves, capture the wounded king, and resolve the matter without arms. Oppression, repeated defeats, hunger, mourning, and many widows follow. Unable to contend by the sword, they humble themselves, cry to God, prosper, raise grain more abundantly, covenant to serve God, and desire baptism. Led by Ammon and his brethren, they leave by night with women, children, flocks, herds, tents, provisions, gold, silver, and precious things. After many days in the wilderness, they arrive in Zarahemla, are delivered from bondage, become subjects of Mosiah, and are baptized by Alma into the church of God.

l: king Laman, The Book of Mosiah
s: King Laman is the ruler of the Lamanites. He covenants with Zeniff to yield Lehi-Nephi and Shilom, but uses cunning, lying craftiness, and fair promises to seek Zeniff’s people’s bondage or destruction. He commands his people to depart, then stirs them up to contend against Zeniff’s people.
